title: How to Raise Kids Who Own Their Faith
excerpt: You cannot hand your child a faith they merely inherit. You can only raise them in conditions where a faith of their own has room to grow.
body:
Every Christian parent fears the same thing: that their child will walk away from the faith. The fear drives some parents to control, to tighten the rules and shrink the questions, believing that a faith held firmly enough by the parent will transfer to the child. It almost never works that way. A faith that is only inherited, never owned, tends to fall off the first time the world pushes hard. The children who keep their faith are usually the ones who were allowed to make it theirs.

You cannot save your child. You were never able to. What you can do is tend the soil, and trust the One who actually grows things.

## Faith caught more than taught

Children absorb the faith you live far more than the faith you explain. They watch whether your religion makes you kinder or harsher, whether you pray when no one is looking, whether grace is something you preach or something you practice on them at the kitchen table. A faith that is real in the ordinary fabric of the home is contagious. A faith that is performed on Sunday and absent on Tuesday teaches them that the whole thing is theater.

This is humbling, because it means the most important curriculum is your own life. Paul could tell the Corinthians to imitate him as he imitated Christ. The question for us is narrower and harder: if my child imitates the faith they actually see in me, where will it take them? That question should shape us before it shapes them.

## Make room for doubt

The parents whose children most often keep the faith are frequently the ones who let their children question it. This feels backward, but it holds. A faith that was never allowed to be questioned was never really owned; it was only borrowed, and borrowed things get returned. When you welcome your child's doubts instead of fearing them, you teach that the faith is sturdy enough to be examined, and that they do not have to choose between honesty and belief.

So when the hard questions come, and they will, do not shut them down. Welcome them. "That is a good question, let's think about it." A child who can bring their doubt to you will keep bringing it, and a doubt brought into the light tends to resolve toward faith far more often than one driven into hiding. The deep guide at /life/raising-children-in-grace and the piece on answering hard questions go further into this. The short version: do not be afraid of their questions. Be afraid of their silence.

## Let it cost something

A faith that costs nothing is worth nothing, and children sense this. If following Jesus in your home means only comfort, never sacrifice, your child learns that faith is a consumer good. But if they see the faith cost you something, generosity that pinches, forgiveness that is hard, honesty when a lie would be easier, telling the truth when it is expensive, they learn that this is real, because real things cost.

Give them ways to live it out, not just believe it. Serve someone together. Give until it is felt. Let them see you choose the harder right over the easier wrong and name why. Faith becomes their own when they have spent something on it. James said faith without works is dead, and a child raised on belief without action is being handed a corpse.

## Aim for relationship, not behavior

It is possible to raise a child who keeps all the rules and knows nothing of God, and many of us have done exactly that without meaning to. If the goal becomes managing behavior, you can produce a moral child with a dead heart, which is the Pharisee's trajectory. The goal is not a well-behaved child. It is a child who knows God, who has met him personally, who prays not to satisfy you but because they have found Someone worth talking to.

So keep pointing past yourself and past the rules to God himself. Pray with them in ways that are real. Read the Bible as a place to meet a Person, not a rulebook to memorize. Tell them what God has done in your own life, including recently, including the hard parts. You are introducing them to Someone, and an introduction is not the same as enforcement.

## This week

Do one thing that lets your child's faith become theirs rather than yours. Welcome a doubt instead of fearing it. Let them see the faith cost you something real and tell them why you paid it. Pray with them in a way that is honest rather than rote. And then loosen your grip, because the thing you are most afraid of is not finally in your hands. Tend the soil this week, and trust the One who grows things to do what you cannot.
